question: How should a trailer's two safety chains be attached to the towing vehicle, according to the Georgia Boat-Ed course?
choice_a: Left hanging loose and uncrossed, coiled to keep them off the pavement
choice_b: Crisscrossed underneath the trailer's coupler, so they can support the coupler if it comes loose from the hitch ball
choice_c: Attached only if the trailer weighs more than 5,000 pounds
choice_d: Wrapped around the license plate bracket rather than the hitch
explanation: Two strong safety chains -- strong enough to hold the combined weight of the vessel, engine, and trailer -- should be crisscrossed underneath the trailer's coupler when attaching them to the towing vehicle, so they can catch and support the coupler if it becomes disconnected.

question: What warning does the Georgia Boat-Ed course give about relying on a trailer's bow winch to hold the vessel in place during transport?
choice_a: The bow winch is always sufficient by itself and no additional straps are needed
choice_b: The bow winch should be completely released before towing to reduce strain
choice_c: Never trust the bow winch alone to hold the vessel onto the trailer -- use tie-down straps and/or safety lines as well
choice_d: Tie-down straps should replace the bow winch entirely and the winch line should be removed before towing
explanation: Before leaving home with a boat and trailer, secure the vessel to the trailer with several tie-down straps and/or safety lines -- never trust the bow winch alone to hold the vessel onto the trailer.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'Before Leaving Home With Your Boat and Trailer'

question: What should a boater confirm about the hitch ball and trailer coupler before towing a boat trailer?
choice_a: That the hitch ball is painted the same color as the trailer
choice_b: That the coupler is at least twice the diameter of the hitch ball
choice_c: Ball and coupler sizes never need to match as long as the coupler locks shut
choice_d: That the size stamped on the towing vehicle's hitch ball matches the size stamped on the trailer's coupler
explanation: Make sure the size stamped on the ball hitch of the towing vehicle is the same size that is stamped on the trailer's coupler; a mismatch can allow the trailer to separate from the tow vehicle.

question: Which type of hitch mounting does the Georgia Boat-Ed course say is preferable for towing a boat trailer?
choice_a: A frame-mounted hitch on the towing vehicle, rather than a bumper-mounted hitch
choice_b: A bumper-mounted hitch, since it is always rated for a heavier load
choice_c: Mounting location is irrelevant as long as safety chains are used
choice_d: A hitch mounted directly to the vehicle's rear axle housing
explanation: A frame-mounted hitch on the towing vehicle is better than a bumper-mounted hitch; if a bumper-mounted hitch must be used, its weight rating should not be exceeded.

question: What can happen if a trailer's tongue weight is too light relative to the combined vessel-and-trailer weight?
choice_a: The towing vehicle's rear wheels lose steering control
choice_b: The trailer can sway or 'fishtail' side-to-side behind the towing vehicle
choice_c: The hitch ball will not fit the coupler
choice_d: The bilge will overfill with water
explanation: Tongue weight should be about 10% of the combined vessel-and-trailer (gross trailer) weight; too little tongue weight lets the trailer fishtail side-to-side, while too much overburdens the tow vehicle's rear wheels and hurts steering control.

question: According to the Georgia Boat-Ed course, what should a driver do periodically while towing a boat trailer on the road?
choice_a: Only stop if a warning light appears on the dashboard
choice_b: Stop only at the final destination, since checking en route wastes time
choice_c: Pull over every hour or so to check the towing vehicle, trailer, tires, trailer coupling, and gear in the vessel
choice_d: Check the trailer only if towing more than 100 miles
explanation: When towing on the road, drive at moderate speeds, avoid sudden maneuvers, and pull over every hour or so to check the towing vehicle, trailer, tires, trailer coupling, and gear in the vessel.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'On the Road With a Trailer'

question: Why should a driver towing a boat trailer make wider turns and allow extra stopping distance?
choice_a: Georgia law requires all trailered vehicles to use the leftmost lane
choice_b: Wider turns are only needed for trailers longer than the average size
choice_c: It has no real effect; standard driving techniques are always sufficient
choice_d: The added length and weight of the trailer change how the vehicle handles and stops
explanation: A trailer's added length and weight mean a driver must make wider turns at corners and curves and allow extra time and distance for stopping and passing other vehicles.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'On the Road With a Trailer'

question: When backing a trailered vessel into the water to launch, how far should the trailer be backed in before lowering and starting the engine?
choice_a: Far enough that the engine's lower unit can be lowered and submerged while the vessel is still on the trailer
choice_b: Only until the trailer tires touch the waterline
choice_c: All the way until the tow vehicle's rear bumper is submerged
choice_d: The engine should never be started until the vessel is fully floating off the trailer
explanation: Back the trailered vessel into the water far enough that the engine's lower unit can be lowered and submerged while the vessel is still on the trailer, so the engine can be started and warmed up before backing further in to float the vessel off.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'Backing the Trailer Into the Water During Launch'

question: What added precaution should a driver take with the towing vehicle while backing a trailer down a launch ramp?
choice_a: Leave the towing vehicle running in reverse gear the whole time
choice_b: Set the towing vehicle's parking brake
choice_c: Disconnect the vehicle's battery before backing down
choice_d: Remove the spare tire to reduce weight on the ramp
explanation: As an added precaution while backing a trailer into the water to launch, always set the parking brake on the towing vehicle.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'Backing the Trailer Into the Water During Launch'

question: About how far should a trailer's rollers or bunks be submerged when backing in to retrieve (load) a vessel back onto the trailer?
choice_a: The trailer should stay entirely out of the water during retrieval
choice_b: The entire trailer, including the axle housings, must be fully submerged
choice_c: Approximately two-thirds of the rollers or bunks submerged in the water
choice_d: Only the trailer's rear light bar needs to touch the water
explanation: To retrieve a vessel, back the trailer into the water so that approximately two-thirds of the rollers or bunks are submerged, then set the parking brake, put the vehicle in park (or first gear), and winch the vessel aboard.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'Retrieving Your Boat Onto a Trailer'

question: Why does the Georgia Boat-Ed course advise against 'power loading' a vessel onto its trailer using engine power?
choice_a: Power loading is faster but voids the vessel's registration
choice_b: It uses too much fuel compared to winching
choice_c: It is not actually discouraged; power loading is the recommended method
choice_d: Propeller wash can erode the ramp's sediment into a hole and deposit a mound behind it, creating hazards for trailers and boats
explanation: Do not power load a vessel onto its trailer using engine power -- the propeller wash can erode ramp sediment into a hole, deposit a mound behind it, and cause trailer tires to get stuck or boats to run aground.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'Do Not Power Load Your Boat'

question: What ramp-courtesy practice does the Georgia Boat-Ed course recommend to avoid blocking a boat ramp?
choice_a: Prepare the vessel for launching, or for the drive home, well away from the ramp, and never leave an unattended vessel or vehicle blocking it
choice_b: Always launch solo and take as much time as needed at the ramp itself
choice_c: Leave the vessel in the launch lane until the towing vehicle is parked
choice_d: Ramp courtesy rules only apply to commercial vessels
explanation: Prepare your vessel for launching or for the drive home well away from the ramp, and never block a ramp with an unattended vessel or vehicle; using two people, or wheel chocks if launching solo, helps keep the process quick for everyone.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'Courtesy on the Boat Ramp'

question: After retrieving a vessel and moving away from the ramp, what does the Georgia Boat-Ed course say a boater should do to avoid spreading aquatic invasive species?
choice_a: Nothing extra is needed once the vessel is out of the water
choice_b: Remove weeds from the trailer and hull and drain the bilge and live wells before leaving the area
choice_c: Only rinse the outside of the hull with lake water
choice_d: Leave weeds attached until the next trip so they dry out naturally in transit
explanation: Once the vessel is on land and away from the ramp, remove weeds from the trailer and hull and drain the bilge and live wells to prevent spreading aquatic invasive species to other waters.
source_note: Georgia Boat-Ed Course, 'Retrieving Your Boat Onto a Trailer'

question: What water temperature does Georgia DNR's Clean, Drain, Dry guidance recommend for cleaning a boat, motor, and trailer before leaving a water access area?
choice_a: Cold water only, since heat can damage marine finishes
choice_b: Room-temperature tap water is sufficient in all cases
choice_c: High-pressure and/or hot water at 120 degrees Fahrenheit or higher
choice_d: Salt water only, regardless of the water body launched into
explanation: Georgia DNR's Clean, Drain, Dry guidance calls for cleaning gear, watercraft, trailer, motor, and equipment with high-pressure and/or hot water at 120 degrees Fahrenheit (50 degrees Celsius) or higher, and removing visible aquatic plants, mussels, other animals, and mud before leaving any water access.
source_note: Georgia DNR, 'Defend Georgia Waters Against Aquatic Invasive Species' (GeorgiaWildlife.com/ans Clean, Drain, Dry guidance)

question: How long does Georgia DNR's Clean, Drain, Dry guidance recommend a boat, trailer, and gear be dried out before launching into a different waterbody?
choice_b: There is no recommended drying period
explanation: Georgia DNR's Clean, Drain, Dry guidance recommends drying everything -- boat, gear, trailer, and equipment -- for at least five days before launching into other waters and landings, to avoid transporting aquatic invasive species between water bodies.
source_note: Georgia DNR, GeorgiaWildlife.com/ans Clean, Drain, Dry guidance

question: Where does Georgia DNR's Clean, Drain, Dry guidance say a boater should drain water from the bilge, motor, and livewell by removing the drain plug?
choice_a: Away from the boat ramp, not into the water access area itself
choice_b: Directly onto the boat ramp surface so it washes into the water
choice_c: It does not matter where the water is drained
choice_d: Only at a certified marina fuel dock
explanation: Georgia DNR's Clean, Drain, Dry guidance directs boaters to drain water from gear, boat, bilge, motor, and livewell by removing the drain plug and opening all water-draining devices away from the boat ramp, not into the water access area.
source_note: Georgia DNR, GeorgiaWildlife.com/ans Clean, Drain, Dry guidance
